Full text

Abstract

Recognition memory is influenced by both the depth of processing during encoding and the congruency of incoming information with existing knowledge. Although both factors have been shown to affect memory performance, their combined influence on the electrophysiological mechanisms underlying recognition remains unclear. The present study investigated how level of processing (LOP) and semantic congruency interact to modulate behavioral performance and event-related potentials (ERPs) associated with recognition memory. Thirty-six healthy young adults completed a recognition task in which encoding required either shallow perceptual judgments or deep semantic judgments, while congruency was manipulated independently. Behavioral performance was assessed using Linear Integrated Speed-Accuracy Scores (LISAS), and ERP components were identified through temporo-spatial principal component analysis. Deep encoding produced significantly better behavioral performance and larger late positive component (LPC) amplitudes than shallow encoding, indicating enhanced recollection-related processing. In contrast, semantic congruency did not significantly influence behavioral performance or LPC activity.

However, congruency strongly modulated the FN400 component, with incongruent items eliciting more negative responses than congruent items. Importantly, this effect interacted with depth of processing, such that congruency-related differences were pronounced following shallow encoding but attenuated following deep encoding. These findings suggest a functional dissociation between early and late stages of recognition memory. While recollection-related activity appears to be primarily driven by goal-directed semantic processing, early neural responses are sensitive to the interaction between encoding demands and schema compatibility. The results support accounts proposing that recognition memory emerges from the dynamic interplay between mismatch detection and semantic integration processes.

1. Introduction

Episodic memory enables the retrieval of personal experiences within their original spatiotemporal context (Tulving, 2002). The formation and subsequent retrieval of these memories depends fundamentally on the cognitive operations engaged during initial encoding (Allan, 2000). In particular, the persistence of a memory trace is determined by the nature of the processing performed during encoding (Buckner & Wheeler, 2001; Craik & Tulving, 1975). Crucially, not all encoding operations contribute equally to later memory performance (Yan et al., 2023).

The Level of Processing (LOP) framework posits that a deeper processing during encoding, specifically, the extraction of meaning from the experience such as judging an item's animacy, leads to more robust and durable memory traces than shallow analysis (Craik, 2002; Craik & Tulving, 1975; Marzi & Viggiano, 2010). Craik and Tulving (1975) demonstrated that the deep advantage stems from the qualitative nature of the task rather than the processing time, resulting in more elaborate and retrievable representations in episodic memory.

Indeed, contemporary research has expanded these classical findings, providing a plausible mechanism for why deep processing is so effective. Current evidence suggests that the deep encoding advantage is driven by the rapid integration of incoming information into preexisting schemas, a process that goes beyond simple repetition (Marzi & Viggiano, 2010; Packard et al., 2020). Recent studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) have identified that deep semantic tasks trigger a form of "schematic resonance" involving the left inferior prefrontal cortex and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) (Van Kesteren et al., 2012). These prefrontal regions coordinate interactions with medial temporal and posterior cortical areas, thereby facilitating the incorporation of new information into existing knowledge structures (Alejandro et al., 2021; Ghosh & Gilboa, 2014). While classical studies described depth of processing as a hierarchy, current frameworks such as the Schema-Linked Interactions between Medial Prefrontal and Medial Temporal Regions (SLIMM) model explain that this process is actually an active search for meaning, whereby the brain prioritizes information that either reinforces internal predictive models or signals a significant prediction error (Alejandro et al., 2021; Ghosh & Gilboa, 2014). This modern perspective clarifies that the 'deep' advantage identified in previous studies arises from the brain's fundamental strategy using past learning to facilitate new information acquisition (Greve et al., 2019). Accordingly, depth-related advantages may be modulated by congruency.

Congruency can be explained by the compatibility of an objective element with previously existing knowledge (Bein et al., 2015; Van Kesteren et al., 2012). Information that conforms to expectations typically enjoys a memory advantage due to easier integration and elaboration (Persaud et al., 2026; Schmidt, 2016). However, the literature also reports an advantage of incongruency under certain conditions. Interestingly, empirical evidence has demonstrated a U-shaped relationship, whereby both congruent and incongruent information can enhance memory performance (Greve et al., 2019). This pattern is often attributed to the distinctiveness of stimuli that violate prior knowledge, which can further promote encoding (Persaud et al., 2026). According to the integration-elaboration account, congruency facilitates the binding of an item to its context only when the encoding task promotes the processing of semantic relationships (Bein et al., 2015). In this way, prior knowledge acts as a scaffold that anchors new experiences more effectively under deep processing conditions (Persaud et al., 2026; Zoellner et al., 2025). This raises the question of how depth of processing and congruency interact to modulate memory encoding and subsequent retrieval.

When an old item is encountered, access to the prior information can range from a rapid and vague feeling of familiarity to the full retrieval of a specific episodic context, referred to as recollection (Yonelinas, 2002). At the neural level, disentangling the overlapping dynamics of these two distinct processes requires a method with high temporal resolution, as recognition memory operations occur within milliseconds. In this regard, the use of eventrelated potentials (ERPs) has led to the identification of two canonical components that have long been interpreted as indexing distinct retrieval mechanisms. Within the first 300-400 ms following the stimulus onset, a mid-frontal negative component (FN400) emerges as a marker of familiarity (Leynes & Mok, 2020) or prediction errors (Voss et al., 2010). Then, between 500-800 ms a late centroparietal positive component (LPC) has been associated to recollection processes (Stróżak et al., 2016; Yonelinas, 2002).

The early FN400 was traditionally regarded as being insensitive to the depth of processing (Curran, 2000; Nyhus & Curran, 2009; Rugg et al., 1998). However, some studies have demonstrated that semantic encoding can enhance this component, particularly when encoding tasks are divided into sessions or blocks (Marzi & Viggiano, 2010). This finding suggests the hypothesis of an early interaction between processing demands and familiarity signals. In contrast, Yan et al. (2023) have demonstrated that LPC has been identified as a key marker of the interaction between encoding goals and retrieval demands. Specifically, it has been demonstrated that deep encoding tasks involving congruity judgements elicit a wider distribution and stronger modulation of LPC effects during retrieval than shallow tasks do (Yan et al., 2023). The hypothesis that semantic congruency provides the necessary schematic resonance to enable deep processing and the formation of high-quality, contextually rich representations has been put forward (Van Kesteren et al., 2012). This hypothesis is consistent with the findings of Craik and Tulving (1975). These representations are subsequently accessed via more extensive and controlled search mechanisms, as indexed by the LPC, rather than relying on an automatic signal (Brod et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2023).

Consequently, the interplay between LPC and congruency determines whether recognition can be resolved early or if the search-intensive process reflected in late posterior activity is required (Ghosh & Gilboa, 2014).

While the individual effects of LOP and congruency are well-documented, their joint influence on electrophysiological mechanism of recognition remains poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear how the depth of processing during encoding modulates the impact of congruency on familiarity and recollection. In addition, there is an ongoing debate as to whether the FN400 reflects familiarity (Yonelinas, 2002) or, alternatively, processes related to information prioritization, such as schematic integration or novelty detection (Leynes & Mok, 2020; Voss et al., 2010).

Therefore, this current study investigates how depth of processing and semantic congruency jointly influence recognition memory, using a paradigm that manipulates two levels of processing (deep vs. shallow) and congruency (congruent vs. incongruent), while recording behavioral performance and ERP components (FN400 and LPC).

The present study formulated three sets of hypotheses according to (1) the effect of congruency, (2) the effect of processing level and (3) their interaction First, we predict a main effect of congruency, such that recognition performance will be better and faster for congruent relative to incongruent items. At the neural level, congruent items are expected to elicit larger FN400 (reflecting enhanced familiarity) and LPC amplitudes (reflecting enhanced recollection).

Second, we predict a main effect of level of processing, such that shallow encoding will lead to lower recognition accuracy and slower response times compared to deep encoding. This effect should also be reflected in decreased FN400 and LPC amplitudes.

Third, we predict an interaction between congruency and level of processing, such that congruency effects will be amplified under deep encoding conditions. This interaction may differentially modulate ERP components, revealing a functional dissociation between familiarity-related (FN400) and recollection-related (LPC) processes.

2. Methods

>Methods

2.1 Sample Size Calculation

In order to calculate the number of participants required for this study, the G*Power software was used (Faul et al., 2007). In the present study, the sample size was calculated using an a priori power analysis for a repeated-measures design, assuming a medium effect size (f = 0.25), a significance level of α = 0.05, and a desired statistical power of 1 -β = 0.80. The analysis was configured for a within-subjects ANOVA with two factors (level of processing and congruency). According to the G*Power output, the total sample size required to achieve the desired power was N = 29 participants (actual power ≈ 0.80).

Because some degree of data loss was expected due to EEG artifacts and preprocessing exclusions, we recruited 36 participants. The final sample consisted of 29 participants.

2.2 Participants

Thirty-six participants were recruited (mean age = 20.2; age range = 18-26; 86% female; 94.4% right-handed). Before starting the experimental session, all participants signed the informed consent form and received instructions on the procedure. The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Universidad Rey Juan Carlos (reference 80420242762024). All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.

For the behavioral analyses, seven participants were excluded as behavioral outliers according to Tukey's interquartile range (IQR) criterion (Tukey, 1977), resulting in a final behavioral sample of 29 participants. Following EEG preprocessing and artifact-rejection procedures, an additional five participants were excluded because an insufficient number of artifact-free trials remained for reliable ERP estimation. Therefore, ERP analyses were conducted on a final sample of 24 participants.

2.3 Procedure and stimuli 200 unique everyday objects and common animals were used in the experiment, and another 20 were used for practical purposes, all taken from the experiment used in Griffiths et al., (2019). Of these, 96 were selected from the BOSS database (Brodeur et al., 2014), and the remaining images were obtained from royalty-free online databases. All images were photographs on a white background and, in order to create two levels of manipulation, a freehand line drawing was made using the free and open-source GNU Image Manipulation Software (http://www.gimp.org/). Therefore, there were a total of 110 line drawings (linear schematic outline) and 110 photographs with a white background (Figure 2A).

For each participant, the stimuli were selected pseudo-randomly, such that stimuli were randomly assigned across encoding and retrieval runs while maintaining a balanced distribution of photographs and line drawings in each one. Approximately 80% of the stimuli were later presented as old items and 20% as new (lure) items during retrieval. Finally, they were divided into animate stimuli (animals) and inanimate stimuli (objects). All photographs and line drawings were presented in the center of the screen with a rescaled size of 500 × 500 pixels. Testing took place in a sound-attenuated, electromagnetically shielded, air-conditioned room. Participants sat approximately 70 cm from a 19-inch monitor (60 Hz refresh rate).

The task was divided into two parts: (1) encoding and (2) retrieval. During (1) encoding, two stimuli were presented with an alternating task. The task alternatives were to answer whether the stimuli were perceptually congruent (whether both were photographs or both were line drawings) or whether the stimuli were semantically congruent (whether both were animate or inanimate). Participants completed 40 encoding trials per run. Each trial was presented for up to 3 s, during which participants responded, and was followed by an inter-trial interval of 1.5 s. The (2) retrieval task was a classic recognition task where they were presented with stimuli and had to answer whether each item was old or a new. Then, we manipulated the level of processing by contrasting perceptual (photograph vs line drawing) and semantic (animate vs inanimate) conditions. Participants completed 100 retrieval trials per run. Each retrieval trial began with a fixation cross presented for a jittered interval between 1.5 and 2 s, followed by the stimulus, which remained onscreen for up to 3 s while participants responded. In between, participants were presented with a task where a fixation cross changed colour and had to count how many times it changed. During the experimental session, participants first completed a practice phase aimed at familiarising themselves with the task, after which the EEG recording began (Figure 2B). The experimental task was programmed in MATLAB using Psychtoolbox, and the source code is publicly available at https://github.com/JMartinGM/MemCongr_Project_Experiment.git. 2.4 Electrophysiological recording Brain electrical activity was recorded with the Brain Vision Recorder software (v.1.0; Brain Products, Germany), using a QuickCap-Neuroscan electrode cap with 59 electrodes (FP1, FP2, AF7, AF3, AFz, AF4, AF8, F7, F3, F1, Fz, F2, F4, F5, F6, F8, FT7, FC5, FC3, FC1, FCz, FC2, FC4, FC6, FT8, TP8, C5, C3, C1, Cz, C2, C4, C6, T8, T7, CP3, CP1, CP5, CPz, CP2, CP4, CP6, P7, P5, P3, P1, Pz, P2, P4, P6, P8, PO7, PO3, POz, PO4, PO8, O1, Oz, and O2) homogeneously distributed over the scalp according to the international 10-10 system.

Two electrodes located on the mastoids were used as a reference. Vertical and horizontal eye movements were monitored by simultaneous electrooculographic (EOG) recordings.

Electrode impedance was kept below 5 kΩ. During acquisition, data were bandpass filtered from 0.02 Hz to 40Hz, and sampled at 500Hz. The EEGLAB (v2025.1.0) (Delorme & Makeig, 2004) toolbox in MATLAB (R2025b 25.2.0.2998904) was used to perform EEG preprocessing. Trials were extracted from -200 ms before stimulus onset to 1500 ms after onset. Eye movements artefacts were removed using independent component analysis (ICA).

On average, 2.0 components per participant (SD = 0.6) were rejected following visual inspection of the ICA decomposition.

A baseline correction and visual inspection of the EEG was also performed to remove epochs with artefacts for subsequent analyses. Epochs with activity amplitude greater than ±70 μV were removed. Participants were included only if at least 70% of their 200 trials were free of artefacts, resulting in an average of 140 (SD = 1.5) clean trials per participant. These trials were subsequently distributed across the four experimental conditions, yielding an average of 33.5 valid trials per condition and participant following epoch-level artefact rejection. Following these preprocessing and quality-control procedures, five participants were excluded because an insufficient number of artifact-free trials remained for reliable ERP estimation. Consequently, the final ERP sample consisted of 24 participants. MATLAB scripts used for this pipeline are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/dinosoldic/EEG-Preproc-ERP.git).

2.5 Data analyzes

2.5.1 Behavioral analysis

Prior to the behavioral analyses, participants with extreme behavioral values were identified using Tukey's interquartile range (IQR) criterion. Observations falling beyond 1.5 × IQR from the first or third quartile were classified as outliers and excluded from subsequent analyses (Tukey, 1977). This procedure resulted in the exclusion of seven participants.

Since individual variability drives adaptive behavioural prioritizing speed over accuracy, this can lead to experimental bias manifesting in either of the two measures (Vandierendonck, 2017). In order to correct for this phenomenon, the raw reaction time (RT) scores were corrected using a linear integrated speed-accuracy scores (LISAS) as follows: where RTj represents the participant's mean RT in a given condition; σRT is the overall standard deviation of RTs; σPE is the overall standard deviation of the percentage of errors (Pes); and PEj is the participant's mean Pes in a given condition.

2.5.2 Detection and characterization of ERPs: temporo-spatial principal component analysis

To detect and characterize ERP components, we applied a two stage temporo-spatial principal component analysis (PCA). This method combines temporal PCA (tPCA) and spatial PCA (sPCA) to separate address temporal and spatial overlap between underlying neural generators. (Dien, 2012).

First, we performed tPCA using a covariance matrix, was applied to detect and quantify the ERP components explaining most of the brain electrical activity variance. The application of this technique has been strongly recommended for these kind of tasks because it allows avoiding the subjectivity of selecting time windows based only on visual inspection of grand-averaged ERPs (this can lead to several types of misinterpretation, especially when high-density montages are employed), representing each ERP component free of the influences of adjacent or subjacent components (see Dien, 2012, for a more detailed description of tPCA procedure and advantages).

In brief, tPCA computes the covariance between all ERP time points, which tends to be high between those time points involved in the same component, and low between those belonging to different components. The tPCA based on a covariance matrix was performed on the averaged waveforms, each being represented by 551 time points (from 0 to 1100 ms averaged epoch). The solution is therefore a set of different factors made up of highly covarying time points, which ideally correspond to ERP components. The temporal factor (TF) score, the tPCA-derived parameter in which extracted temporal factors (TFs) may be quantified, is linearly related to the amplitude of ERP components. The decision on the number of factors to extract was carried out through the application of the scree test (Cliff, 1987)Promax rotation was applied in order to select temporal factors as recommended (Cohen, 2014; Dien, 2012).

Because ERP components can also overlap spatially, each temporal factor was subsequently decomposed into their main spatial regions of spatial factors (SFs) At any given time point, different neural processes (and hence, different electrical signals) may concur, and the recording at any scalp location at that moment represents the electrical balance of these distinct neural processes. While tPCA allows representing a complex superposition of different overlapping electrical potentials in time, the sPCA separates the ERP components along the electrodes located on the scalp (and hence, different regions). In this sense, each SF would ideally reflect one of the concurrent neural processes underlying each TF. This configuring and quantifying scalp regions system is preferable to an a priori subdivision into fixed scalp regions for all components, since sPCA demarcates scalp regions according to the real behaviorof each scalp-point recording. Frequently, the components fluctuate differently depending on the scalp area analyzed, which can produce an opposite polarity, even react differently to experimental manipulation. This regional grouping was also determined through a covariance matrix-based sPCA and the decision on the number of factors to extract also was carried out through the application of the scree test. Also, Promax rotation was applied in order to select spatial factors (Dien, 2010 (Dien, , 2012)). Therefore, the preprocessing analyzes of ERPs comprised both the tPCA and sPCA. The resulting temporalspatial components were then submitted to 2 x 2 repeated measures ANOVAs reflecting the experimental manipulation, with congruency and level of processing as within-subject factors.

2.6 Detection and characterization of ERPs

To test whether the effect of level of processing and the effect of congruency during the retrieval process, each participant completed the task for every condition (Shallow Congruent, Shallow Incongruent, Deep Congruent and Deep Incongruent). The analyzes were carried out using a series of 2 x 2 repeated measures ANOVAs, which included the level of processing (shallow and deep) and the effect of congruency (congruent and incongruent) as factors.

Effect sizes were calculated using the eta-squared technique (η² p). Post hoc comparisons were performed to determine the significance of the pairwise contrasts, using the Bonferroni test (alpha = 0.05). All statistical analyzes described in this section were performed with Jamovi (2.6.44. Computer Software).

3. Results

>Results

3.1 Behavioural results

The experiment used a 2x2 design in which all participants encoded stimuli for all conditions: level of processing condition (shallow and deep) and for the congruency condition (congruent and incongruent). As shown in Figure 2, a significant main effect of level of processing on LISAS was found [(F 1,28) = 22.9, p<.001, η²p = 0.45]. Mean analyzes revealed higher LISAS scores in shallow compared to deep conditions (Shallow: M = 3.98, SE = 0.31; Deep: M = 3.64, SE = 0.30). No significant effect of congruency was found, [F(1, 28) = 2.03, p = .165], nor was there a significant interaction, [F(1, 28) = 0.014, p = .96.]

3.2 ERP results

To identify and subsequently quantify the FN400 and LPC components of the ERPs, a temporospatial principal component analysis (stPCA) was performed.

Following tPCA, four temporal factors were extracted from the ERPs and subjected to Promax rotation. The extracted factors explained 91.9% of the total variance (TF1: 38.79%, TF2: 31.03%, TF3: 19.16%, TF4: 2.92%).

The topographic distribution of TF1 allowed us to associate it with the FN400 component, characterised by a predominance over central-frontal regions. In contrast, TF3 showed a centro-parietal distribution consistent with the LPC component, whereas TF2 and TF4 displayed earlier and more posterior patterns compatible with perceptual components (P2).

After the application of sPCA, each temporal factor was decomposed into three spatial factors, each reflecting a distinct scalp distribution. Specifically, only the spatial factors derived from TF1 and TF3 showed the expected combination of latency and scalp topography required to identify them as FN400 and LPC components, respectively. The remaining spatial factors showed different temporal or topographic characteristics and were therefore not considered further in the analysis.

The FN400 component (TF1SF3), characterized by a central topography (Figure 3A-B), showed a significant main effect of Congruency [F(1, 23) = 48.40, p < .001, η²p = .678], with lower component scores for incongruent than congruent stimuli (Congruent: M ≈ 1.08-1.07; Incongruent: M ≈ -1.95 to -0.34). A main effect of level of processing was also found, [F(1, 23) = 39.00, p < .001, η²p = .629], with lower scores under shallow than deep processing. Additionally, the interaction between congruency and level of processing was significant [F(1, 23) = 37.50, p < .001, η²p = .62], reflecting a larger congruency effect under shallow (M = 1.08 vs. -1.95) than deep processing (M = 1.07 vs. -0.34).

ERP waveforms (Figure 3C) averaged across the central electrodes that contributed the highest weights to the component (Cz, C1, C2). Congruent stimuli elicited more positive amplitudes than incongruent stimuli, with a larger difference under shallow processing than under deep processing. Mean component scores (Figure 3D) were similar (p > 0.05) for congruent conditions across levels of processing. In contrast, incongruent conditions differed across levels, with lower scores under shallow than deep processing.

Post hoc comparisons (Table 1) indicated that incongruent stimuli had lower scores than congruent stimuli under shallow processing [ΔM = 3.03, t(23) = 9.06, p < .001] and deep processing [ΔM = 1.41, t(23) = 4.10, p = .003]. Congruent stimuli did not differ across levels of processing [ΔM = 0.02, t(23) = 0.12, p = .999]. Incongruent stimuli showed lower scores under shallow than deep processing [ΔM = -1.61, t(23) = -7.45, p < .001]. 389

Regarding the LPC component (TF3SF3) with a centro-parietal topography (see Figures 5A 390 and 5B), a significant main effect of level of processing was observed [F (1,23) =42.31, 391 p<.001, η²p=.648], reflecting greater component amplitudes for deep processing than for 392 shallow processing (see Figure 5C). However, no significant main effect of congruency was 393 found [F (1,23) =0.0155, p=.902], nor was there a significant interaction between level of 394 processing and congruency [F (1,23) =0.6246, p=.437], indicating that the effect of depth of 395 processing did not change as a function of congruency. 396

4. Discussion

Our results show that depth of processing was the main determinant of behavioural performance and recollection-related activity (LPC), whereas semantic congruency leaves these late measures unaffected. However, congruency modulated early neural responses (FN400), where it interacted with Level of Processing (LOP), particularly for incongruent items (Craik & Tulving, 1975; Otten, 2001).

These findings confirm that semantic encoding tasks, such as animacy judgments, produce more robust memory traces that support recollection (Craik & Tulving, 1975; Packard et al., 2020). Importantly, this advantage does not appear to depend simply on semantic richness, but rather on the type of processing engaged during encoding. In particular, deep processing may promote an active search for meaning that supports the construction of structured representations (Packard et al., 2020).

From this perspective, LOP effects may reflect the extent to which encoding engages integration processes. This shifts the emphasis away from a purely hierarchical notion of depth (Greve et al., 2019; Van Kesteren et al., 2012).

At a neural level, the LPC modulation mirrored the behavioural results, showing a clear modulation for deep encoding but no effect of congruency. This supports the idea that recollection depends mainly on goal-directed semantic processing rather than schema compatibility (Otten, 2001; Yan et al., 2023).

Contrary to our initial predictions, semantic congruency did not significantly influence behavioural performance or LPC amplitudes. This suggests that schema compatibility alone is not sufficient to enhance memory when encoding already involves deep semantic processing (Bein et al., 2015; Greve et al., 2019). One possible explanation is that the animacy task itself was sufficiently demanding to ensure high-quality encoding, making any additional benefit of congruency less relevant. In this case, memory performance may depend more on the processing goals imposed by the task than on the passive match between incoming information and existing knowledge (Greve et al., 2019).

However, the absence of behavioural effects does not imply that congruency was irrelevant.

Decision-related factors may mask underlying mnemonic differences. For example, schemaconsistent items may lead to more conservative response criteria due to their overlap with previous knowledge, reducing apparent differences across conditions (Brod et al., 2015).

Overall, these results suggest that the influence of congruency depends on the conditions under which encoding occurs, rather than acting as a general facilitator of memory (Bein et al., 2015).

In term of neural mechanism, congruency modulated early processing, as reflected in the FN400. Incongruent items elicited more negative amplitudes, consistent with prediction error or mismatch detection (Leynes et al., 2024; Leynes & Mok, 2020; Mecklinger & involve both early evaluation and later integration, depending on encoding demands (Ghosh & Gilboa, 2014).

These findings are consistent with models that emphasize the interaction between previous knowledge and incoming information during memory formation, including predictive processing frameworks and schema-based accounts such as SLIMM (Henson & Gagnepain, 2010; Van Kesteren et al., 2012). Within this perspective, deep processing may engage integration mechanisms that incorporate new information into existing knowledge structures (Brod et al., 2015; Van Kesteren et al., 2012), whereas congruency effects depend on whether such integration processes are activated (Bein et al., 2015).

Importantly, this suggests that memory performance reflects not only the presence of prior knowledge, but how that knowledge is used during encoding (Greve et al., 2019). This framework may help explain mixed findings in the literature regarding congruency.

Some studies report advantages for schema-consistent information (Bein et al., 2015; Craik & Tulving, 1975; Greve et al., 2019), whereas others find benefits for incongruent or distinctive stimuli (Macias & Persaud, 2024; Verguts & Notebaert, 2009).

These discrepancies may reflect differences in task demands and encoding goals, which determine whether processing emphasizes mismatch detection or integration mechanisms (Ferreira & Wimber, 2023).

However, it is important to note that, in the present study, the operationalization of both depth of processing and semantic congruency relied on relatively simple categorical distinctions (perceptual vs. semantic judgments; animate vs. inanimate classifications).

While these manipulations are standard in the literature, they may confound processing depth with task demands or decision complexity, making it difficult to disentangle whether the observed effects reflect depth per se or differences in attentional engagement (Bein et al., 2015; Craik, 2002; Marzi & Viggiano, 2010; Otten, 2001; Packard et al., 2017). Moreover, the use of basic categorical associations may not fully capture the richness and complexity of real-world schemas, potentially limiting the ecological validity of the findings and attenuating the magnitude of congruency effects, particularly under deep encoding conditions. In addition, the final ERP analyses were conducted on a reduced sample of 24 participants following artifact rejection procedures, which may have limited sensitivity to detect smaller effect.

Future research should aim to manipulate the qualitative nature of memory schemas. The transition from the controlled associations used here to more complex, real-world knowledge structures should be investigated, in order to determine the boundary conditions under which deep processing consistently overrides the benefits of schemas. It will be essential to use cross-task paradigms that directly compare recall and recognition across diverse stimulus domains if we are to understand the generalizability of the U-shaped function of memory and its neural correlates. Furthermore, adopting model-based approaches will allow for a more precise formalisation of the executive functions, such as selective attention and inhibitory control, that dictate when the memory system shifts between mismatch detection and schematic integration. By demonstrating a functional dissociation between early and late ERP components, our results show that while recollection-related activity (LPC) is driven predominantly by goaldirected semantic analysis, early evaluative processes (FN400) are sensitive to the interaction between task demands and schema compatibility. Conclusively, these findings shift the focus from a rigid, hierarchical view of memory depth toward an interactive framework where prior knowledge is dynamically deployed based on the specific task constraints.

The resources supporting this study are publicly available through the Open Science Framework (OSF) repository: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/HGEA7 . The repository includes the raw and processed EEG data organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification, the behavioral data used in the reported analyses, and the experimental materials (stimuli and task-related resources). Analysis scripts are not hosted in the OSF repository and are instead publicly available through the GitHub repositories referenced in the Methods section.

Bader, 2020). This suggests that congruency affects early evaluative processes even when it does not translate into behavioural differences or recollection-related activity. However, congruency effects on the FN400 were not uniform, but depended on depth of processing.

The key finding of this study is the interaction between LOP and congruency. Specifically, congruency effects were prominent under shallow encoding conditions but became attenuated under deep encoding. This pattern suggests that congruency does not independently enhance memory. Instead, its effects depend on the type of processing engaged during encoding. Under shallow processing, the system appears more sensitive to mismatches, and incongruent items produce stronger FN400 (Leynes & Mok, 2020; Mecklinger & Bader, 2020). In contrast, under deep processing, semantic analysis allows the integration of incongruent items, reducing their discrepancy (Bein et al., 2015; Packard et al., 2020).

In this sense, it seems that depth of processing determines whether the system primarily detects mismatches or engages in integration processes (Greve et al., 2019).

In contrast, the FN400 showed a significant interaction between LOP and congruency. This findings is consistent with the view that the FN400 may reflect the evaluation of incoming information relative to expectations, rather than a simple measure of memory strength (Mecklinger & Bader, 2020; Stróżak et al., 2016). Under shallow encoding, incongruent items elicited more negative amplitudes, consistent with prediction error or mismatch detection (Leynes et al., 2024; Leynes & Mok, 2020). Under deep encoding, this effect was reduced, mainly because incongruent items became more positive.

Together, these findings support a functional dissociation, whereby FN400 may reflect early evaluative processes, including prediction error and processing fluency (Leynes & Mok, 2020; Mecklinger & Bader, 2020), whereas LPC reflects later integration and recollection processes (Stróżak et al., 2016; Yonelinas, 2002). Figure 1.

Figure 1. Experimental design and trial structure. A) Illustrations of the orthogonal stimulus design. Objects (N=220) varied independently along two dimensions: a perceptual dimension, where the items were presented either as a photograph or as a line drawing. And a semantic dimension, where objects belong to either the animate or inanimate category. The combination of these factors produced a fully balanced stimulus set. B) Schematic representation of the paradigm. During the encoding phase, participants studied object-object pairs and completed a categorization judgment on each trial based on either the perceptual (photograph vs line drawing) or semantic (animate vs inanimate) features of the object. During the retrieval phase, objects were presented individually and participants judged whether each item was old or new. Button icons indicate the moments at which reaction times where recorded.

Figure 3 FN400 component. PCA Results. (A) Temporal PCA factor loadings showing the component associated with the FN400 (TF1 highlighted). (B) Spatial weights of the corresponding spatiotemporal factor (TFS1SF3), revealing a centrotopographic distribution. (C) Grand-average ERPs (smoothed, 25 ms) extracted from central electrodes (Cz, C1, C2) across conditions, illustrating amplitude differences in the 300-500 ms time window. For visualization purposes, the standard error of the mean (SEM) is not displayed. Congruent stimuli elicited more positive amplitudes than incongruent stimuli, with a larger congruency effect under shallow compared to deep processing, consistent with the observed main effects and interaction at the component level. (D) Interaction between level of processing and congruency on FN400 component scores. Mean component scores (± SEM) are plotted as a function of level of processing (shallow, deep) and congruency (congruent, incongruent). Congruent conditions show comparable values across processing levels. In contrast, incongruent conditions diverge markedly, with more negative component scores under shallow processing and a shift toward less negative values under deep processing, illustrating the interaction between congruency and processing depth.
